subject: math
domain: Number and Quantity — The Complex Number System
cluster: Perform arithmetic operations with complex numbers
description: Students add, subtract, and multiply complex numbers written in standard form $a+bi$, using the relation $i^2=-1$ together with the commutative, associative, and distributive properties. They combine like terms (real with real, imaginary with imaginary) for sums and differences, distribute and FOIL for products, and always reduce $i^2$ to $-1$ so that every result is written in the form $a+bi$ with $a$ and $b$ real. They also recognize and use the special product $(a+bi)(a-bi)=a^2+b^2$ for conjugates, and simplify higher powers of $i$ by reducing the exponent modulo $4$.
subSkills: Add two complex numbers by combining real parts and imaginary parts: $(a+bi)+(c+di)=(a+c)+(b+d)i$
Subtract two complex numbers by distributing the negative sign before combining like terms
Multiply a real scalar or a pure imaginary number by a complex number using the distributive property
Multiply two binomial complex numbers using FOIL or distribution, then replace $i^2$ with $-1$
Reduce $i^2=-1$ (and use $i^3=-i$, $i^4=1$) so the final answer is written as $a+bi$
Simplify a power of $i$ such as $i^{n}$ by reducing the exponent modulo $4$
Multiply a complex number by its conjugate to obtain the real value $a^2+b^2$
Express every result in standard form $a+bi$ with real $a$ and $b$, including pure-real ($b=0$) and pure-imaginary ($a=0$) cases

problemArchetypes.name: Powers of i
problemArchetypes.example: Simplify $i^{23}$. Reduce the exponent mod $4$: $23=4\cdot5+3$, so $i^{23}=i^3=-i$.

Easy.description: Single-operation, one-step problems. Addition or subtraction of two complex numbers in standard form, or a simple scalar/pure-imaginary product with at most one $i^2\to-1$ substitution. No nested operations and small integer coefficients.
constraints: Exactly one operation: a single addition, a single subtraction, or a single product with one factor real or pure imaginary
Coefficients are small integers with absolute value $\leq 6$
At most one $i^2$ appears and reduces directly to $-1$
No exponents on binomials and no powers of $i$ beyond $i^2$
Answer is a clean $a+bi$ with integer $a$ and $b$

Medium.description: Two linked steps. Full binomial-times-binomial products requiring FOIL and an $i^2$ reduction, squares of a complex number, conjugate products, or simplifying a moderate power of $i$. Each problem is still a single archetype but requires the distributive property plus combining like terms.
constraints: Product of two binomials, a square $(a+bi)^2$, or a conjugate product
Requires applying the distributive property (FOIL) and then replacing $i^2$ with $-1$
May ask to simplify $i^n$ for a moderate exponent ($n\leq 30$) using exponent mod $4$
Coefficients are integers with absolute value $\leq 10$
Answer must be collected into standard form $a+bi$ with integer parts

Hard.description: Multi-step synthesis. Chained operations combining a product with an additional sum or difference, expressions that mix higher powers of $i$ with multiplication, products of three factors, or problems that require recognizing when a result is purely real or purely imaginary. Student must sequence operations correctly and reduce all powers of $i$.
constraints: At least two distinct operations chained, e.g. multiply then subtract, or two products combined
May include a higher power of $i$ (such as $i^3$ or $i^{n}$, $n>4$) inside a larger expression that must be reduced before combining
May involve a product of three factors or a squared binomial embedded in a larger expression
Coefficients may be larger integers or require careful sign tracking across several terms
May ask the student to justify or state whether the simplified result is real, imaginary, or general, or to identify which property (commutative/associative/distributive) was used at a given step

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats $i^2$ as $+1$ (or leaves $i^2$ unsimplified) instead of $-1$
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $(2+3i)(4-i)$ keeps $-3i^2$ as $-3$ or uses $i^2=+1$ and reports $8+10i-3=5+10i$ instead of $11+10i$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student forgets to distribute the subtraction sign across both terms of the second complex number
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $(7-3i)-(2+6i)$ subtracts only the real part and writes $5+3i$ (or $5-3i+6i$), failing to negate the $+6i$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student adds or combines the real part with the imaginary part as if they were like terms
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $(3+4i)+(5-2i)$ merges everything into a single number such as $10i$ or $10+0i$, treating $a$ and $b$ as combinable

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student multiplies complex numbers component-wise, multiplying reals together and imaginaries together
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $(2+3i)(4-i)$ computes $(2\cdot4)+(3\cdot(-1))i=8-3i$ instead of using FOIL to get $11+10i$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student mishandles the square of a binomial, dropping the middle cross term
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $(3-2i)^2$ writes $9+4i^2=9-4=5$ (or $9+4=13$), omitting the $-12i$ cross term

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student gives a sign error on the conjugate product, treating it like a difference of squares with $i^2$ left as $-$ incorrectly
Student reduces powers of $i$ with the wrong cycle or wrong residue
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $i^{23}$ reports $i$ or $1$ (using $23\bmod 4$ incorrectly or assuming a cycle length other than $4$) instead of $i^3=-i$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student performs chained operations in the wrong order or forgets to apply a later operation to every term
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $(1+2i)(3-i)-(4+i)$ stops after the product at $5+5i$ and forgets to subtract $(4+i)$, or subtracts only the real part, giving $1+5i$ instead of $1+4i$
